title: Honor, simply
hook: Epictetus on reverence: think rightly of the gods and keep offerings honest and plain (Enchiridion 31)

segments.voice: Yesterday: kathēkon, the fitting act, measured by the relationship. Your line was what the role asks. Which duty did you do, and for whom? Day three hundred sixty-three.

A small clay cup of wine, poured out on the ground before a meal. A handful of the first barley of the harvest, set at a household shrine. In Epictetus' world, ordinary families did things like this every week, the way some families today light a candle, say grace, or leave flowers at a grave. The handbook doesn't skip over it. Section thirty-one is about reverence, and what's striking is how little it asks for. Two things. Think rightly. Give plainly. Today: honor, simply.
screen: `A CUP POURED ON THE GROUND.` → `THE FIRST BARLEY AT THE SHRINE.` → `HONOR, SIMPLY.`

segments.voice: First, the thinking. The most important part of piety, Epictetus says, is to hold right opinions about the gods: that they exist, and that they govern the whole well and justly. That's his belief, a Stoic's. People on their own path hold many different views here, and this lesson is about the shape of his advice more than the content of his creed. Second, why the thinking matters. Once you hold that view, he says, you can follow what happens willingly, and you'll never blame the gods. But only if you put good and bad in what's up to you. If you put them in outside things, then every time you miss what you wanted, you'll feel cheated, and you'll resent whoever you think is in charge. He gives a hard example from the old stories: Eteocles and Polynices, brothers who killed each other over the throne of Thebes, because each thought the crown was the good. Farmers, sailors and merchants complain at the sky for the same reason. Third, the giving. Pour the libations, make the offerings, give the first fruits, he says, according to the custom of your ancestors. And do it purely. Not carelessly. Not sloppily. Not stingily. And not beyond what you can afford. Fourth, why it travels. You may not share his gods, or any gods. But most of us hold something sacred: a faith, the memory of a grandmother, a mountain, a quiet morning. Epictetus' advice still fits. Don't make it a show, and don't let it go shabby. Honor it honestly, within your means, in the way you were given. Simple isn't the same as small.
screen: `FIRST: THINK RIGHTLY OF THE GODS.` · `MISPLACED GOOD BREEDS RESENTMENT.` · `NOT CARELESS, STINGY, OR TOO MUCH.` · `HONEST AND PLAIN, WHATEVER YOU HOLD.` · then, large: `HONESTLY, SIMPLY.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and breathe. Ask yourself what you hold sacred. It might be God, or a tradition, or a person who's gone, or the sea, or something you don't have a name for. Let one come to mind. Now picture a plain way to honor it today. Not a grand gesture. A candle lit. A minute of silence. A photo dusted. A walk to the water. If you pray, a prayer you already know. Choose one, and see yourself doing it, carefully and without fuss. The bell holds the time.
Honor. In Enchiridion thirty-one, reverence comes in two parts: right thinking, and offerings made honestly, plainly, and within your means. Today's word.
Your line: honestly, simply. Make one small, honest gesture toward what you hold sacred today, no bigger than it needs to be, and no smaller. Day three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Ancient Stoics took part in their city's customary offerings, plainly and within their means; people on their own path today often keep a small, simple ritual for whatever they hold sacred.

fork.setup: the harvest is in, and your family's custom is to offer the first fruits. how does Epictetus say to give them?
options: as lavishly as possible, so everyone sees.
purely, not carelessly or stingily, and not beyond your means.
skip it. the gods don't need barley.
fork.reveal: he keeps the custom of the ancestors, and asks only that it be done honestly and plainly, within what you can afford.

original.note: Greek: reverence or piety, the subject of Enchiridion 31.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoics didn't care about religion.
what it means: Epictetus asks for right thinking about the gods and offerings made honestly and plainly.
what a scholar hears: he ties piety to his core teaching. put good only in what's up to you, or you'll end up blaming the gods.

sources.ref: Eteocles and Polynices (e.g. Aeschylus, Seven Against Thebes)

notes: Enchiridion 31 paraphrased: right opinions (the gods exist and govern well and justly); yield and follow willingly; good and bad only in what is up to us; Polynices and Eteocles; farmer, sailor, merchant; libations, sacrifices and first fruits according to ancestral custom, purely, not slovenly, carelessly or meanly, nor beyond one's means. Confirm.

The script frames Epictetus' theology as his belief and invites people on their own path to apply the 'honest and plain' shape to whatever they hold sacred. Confirm this is fair to Stoic piety and welcoming to listeners with other or no beliefs.
Greek εὐσέβεια: confirm it is the word Epictetus uses at the opening of Ench. 31 and the pronunciation.
